# Problem 1
```{r p1_cleaning}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")

ny_noaa = ny_noaa |> 
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month"), 4) |> 
  separate(month, into= c("month", "day"), 3) |> 
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    month = as.numeric(month)*-1,
    day = as.numeric(day)*-1,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax),
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin)
  )

#According to the codebook, precipitation is reported in tenths of mm, so we need to divide by 10; tmax and tmin are also in tenths of degrees C

ny_noaa = 
  ny_noaa |> 
  mutate(
    prcp = prcp/10,
    tmax = tmax/10,
    tmin = tmin/10
  )
```

The `ny_noaa` dataset contains daily weather data for New York from `r min(pull(ny_noaa, year))` to `r max(pull(ny_noaa, year))`. The variables include the date, maximum and minimum temperatures,
precipitation, and snowfall (depth and amount). There are `r scales::comma(nrow(ny_noaa))` observations in this dataset. The average values for each variable are as follows:

- the average maximum temperature is `r round(mean(pull(ny_noaa, tmax), na.rm = TRUE), 1)` degrees Celsius

- the average minimum temperature is `r round(mean(pull(ny_noaa, tmin), na.rm = TRUE), 1)` degrees Celsius

- the average precipitation is `r round(mean(pull(ny_noaa, prcp), na.rm = TRUE), 1)` mm

- the average snowfall is `r round(mean(pull(ny_noaa, snow), na.rm = TRUE), 1)` mm

- the average snowfall depth is `r round(mean(pull(ny_noaa, snwd), na.rm = TRUE), 1)` mm


There is quite a bit of missing data in this dataset. There are,

- `r scales::comma(sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmax))))` missing values for maximum temperature (`r round(sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmax)))/nrow(ny_noaa)*100, 2)` % of the data)

- `r scales::comma(sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmin))))` missing values for minimum temperature (`r round(sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmin)))/nrow(ny_noaa)*100, 2)` % of the data)

- `r scales::comma(sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, prcp))))` missing values for precipitation (`r round(sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, prcp)))/nrow(ny_noaa)*100, 2)` % of the data)

- `r scales::comma(sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, snow))))` missing values for snowfall (`r round(sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, snow)))/nrow(ny_noaa)*100, 2)` % of the data)

- `r scales::comma(sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, snwd))))` missing values for snowfall depth (`r round(sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, snwd)))/nrow(ny_noaa)*100, 2)` % of the data)

Thus, missing data is clearly an issue in this dataset.

```{r snow_common_vals}
ny_noaa |>
  group_by(snow) |>
  summarize(
    count=n()
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(count)) |> 
  head(5)
```

The most commonly observed values are close to 0 for snowfall. Specifically, the most common values (aside from NA) are 0, 25, and 13 mm. This is because this weather data is taken for every day of the year, and in NY, there is only snow a couple months of the year, and there only tends to be a couple of days of heavy snowfall a year. 25mm is approximately 1 inch, and 13mm is approximately 0.5 inches, which are both reasonable amounts of snowfall for a single day in NY. Additionally, measurements are often captured in inches and then converted to mm, which could explain why 1 and 0.5 inches are the most common values aside from 0.

```{r june_july_maxtemp}
ny_noaa |> 
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |> 
  mutate(
    month = case_match(
      month,
      1 ~ "January",
      7 ~ "July"
    )
  ) |> 
  group_by(id, year, month) |> 
  summarize(avg_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = avg_tmax, group = id)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_smooth(aes(group = NULL))+ #removing grouping so there is one overall smooth line rather than a line for each station
  facet_grid(.~month) + 
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Max Temperature (C)"
  )
```

The values appear to be much lower in January than July. They also tend to be more variable in January. There 
appears to be one outlier in July around 14 degrees C in 1988 (with a couple other points being potential outliers). It is hard to tell if any of the January values would be considered outliers without conducting further analyses. The graphs show a cyclical pattern rather than a long-term change over time, consistent with what we would expect for weather from year to year.

```{r tmax_min_plot, fig.height = 12}
p1_i_plot = ny_noaa |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) + 
  geom_hex() + 
  labs(
    x = "Minimum Temperature (C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (C)"
  ) +
  theme(legend.text = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

p1_ii_plot = ny_noaa |> 
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = factor(year))) + 
  geom_density_ridges() + 
  labs(x = "Snowfall (mm)", y = "Year") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size=6))

p1_i_plot + p1_ii_plot
```

According to the hex plot, there appears to be a strong linear trend between maximum and minimum temperatures. There appears to be a few stations for which tmax is reported as lower than tmin, indicating errors in the data. There are also some extreme values (i.e. 60 degrees C) that are not plausible for NY.

Additionally, each year shows higher counts of lower snowfall amounts. In most years, there appear to be a couple days with bigger snowfalls (around 80mm), which are likely from the 1-2 storms we have each year. Otherwise, most snowfall clusters between 0-40mm. 

# Problem 2
```{r p2_data}
# for nhanes_demog, 1 = male, 2 = female, 1 = Less than high school, 2 =  High school equivalent, 3  = More than high school

nhanes_demog = read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = case_match(
      sex,
      1 ~ "Male",
      2 ~ "Female"
    ),
    education = case_match(
      education,
      1 ~ "Less than high school",
      2 ~ "High school equivalent",
      3 ~ "More than high school"
      )
    ) |> 
  mutate(
    education = fct_relevel(education, c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school")),
    sex = fct_relevel(sex, c("Male", "Female"))
  ) |> 
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
  drop_na()

nhanes_accel = read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  pivot_longer(
    starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(minute)
  )

nhanes = left_join(nhanes_demog, nhanes_accel, by = "seqn")
```

```{r sex_ed_tbl}
nhanes_demog |> 
  count(education, sex) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n) |> 
  knitr::kable()
```

Out of the three levels of education, "More than high school" has the highest number of males and females. There are more females in the "Less than high school" category than the "High echool equivalent" category. There are more males with "High school equivalent" than females, but in the other categories the numbers are pretty similar. There are more males than females in the sample.

```{r sex_ed_age_plot}
nhanes |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=sex, y = age))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  facet_grid(.~education) + 
  labs(
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age"
  )
```

The distributions of all of the groups overlap substantially. In general, people with more than high school educations are a bit younger, though the quantiles overlap substantially. 

```{r activity_age_plot}
nhanes |> 
  group_by(seqn, sex, education, age) |> 
  summarize(total_mims = sum(mims), .groups = "drop") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_mims, color = sex))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE)+
  facet_grid(.~education)+
  labs(
    x = "Age",
    y = "Total Activity (MIMS)"
  )
```

Total activity declines with age in all three education groups, most steeply among those with less than a high school education. Women generally have higher total activity than men in the “High school equivalent” and “More than high school” groups, while in “Less than high school” the pattern is mixed, with men slightly higher around ages 50–60.

```{r activity_time_plot}
nhanes |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = minute/60, y = mims, color = sex)) + 
  geom_smooth() + 
  facet_grid(.~education) +
  labs(x = "Hour of the day", y = "Activity (MIMS)")
```

In all three graphs, activity happens in the middle of the day. Females have slightly higher activity than males. There does not appear to be any major differences activity across education groups, aside from slightly higher activity levels in people with less than a high school education. Where "High school equivalent" and "More than high school" tend to plateau through the day (approximately 10am to 8pm), "less than high school" has more of a point around 12pm.

# Problem 3
```{r citibike_data}
citibike_0120 = read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv") |> 
  mutate(month = "Jan",
         year = "2020")
citibike_0720 = read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv")|> 
  mutate(month = "July",
         year = "2020")
citibike_0124 = read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv")|> 
  mutate(month = "Jan",
         year = "2024")
citibike_0724 = read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv")|> 
  mutate(month = "July",
         year = "2024")

citibike = bind_rows(citibike_0120, citibike_0720, citibike_0124, citibike_0724) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    month = fct_relevel(month, c("Jan", "July")),
    year = fct_relevel(year, c("2020", "2024")),
    rideable_type = fct_relevel(rideable_type, c("classic_bike", "electric_bike")),
    weekdays = fct_relevel(weekdays, c("Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday"))
  )
```

The `citibike` dataset has `r scales::comma(nrow(citibike))` observations and `r scales::comma(ncol(citibike))` variables. The variables include the ride ID, start and end times, bike type, duration, start and end station names and IDs, rider type (member or casual), year, month, and day of the week.

There are:

- `r scales::comma(sum(pull(citibike, rideable_type) == "classic_bike"))` rides on classic bikes and `r scales::comma(sum(pull(citibike, rideable_type) == "electric_bike"))` rides on electric bikes in the dataset.

- `r scales::comma(sum(pull(citibike, member_casual) == "member"))` rides by members and `r scales::comma(sum(pull(citibike, member_casual) == "casual"))` rides by casual riders in the dataset

- `r scales::comma(nrow(citibike_0120))` rides from January 2020, `r scales::comma(nrow(citibike_0720))` rides from July 2020, `r scales::comma(nrow(citibike_0124))` rides from January 2024, and `r  scales::comma(nrow(citibike_0724))` rides from July 2024.

- the average duration of rides is `r round(mean(pull(citibike,duration), na.rm = TRUE), 2)` minutes.

```{r rides_members}
citibike |> 
  group_by(year, month, member_casual) |> 
  summarize(
    total_rides = n()
  ) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = total_rides
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits=2)
```

From this table, it is evident that both members and casual riders tend to ride more in July than January. 
Additionally, across both casual riders and members, rides increased between 2020 and 2024. Overall, there are
more rides by members than casual riders across all groups.

```{r common_startstations}
citibike |> 
  filter(year == "2024", month == "July") |> 
  group_by(start_station_name) |> 
  summarize(
    total_rides = n()
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(total_rides)) |>
  head(n=5) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits=2)
```

```{r duration_per_day}
citibike |> 
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |> 
  summarize(
    median_ride_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_ride_duration, color = month, group = month)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() + 
  facet_grid(.~year) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)"
  )
```

From these plots, it is evident that the median ride duration is longer in July than January in both 2020 and 2024. Additionally, the median ride duration is longer in 2020 than 2024. In July of both years, the median ride duration tends to be longest on weekends and shortest on weekdays. In January, though, in 2020 the median ride duration is higher on weekends, but in 2024, it is relatively constant, with the longest median ride duration of Thursday-Saturday. 

```{r duration_biketype}
citibike |> 
  filter(year == "2024") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = rideable_type , y = duration, fill = member_casual)) + 
  geom_violin() + 
  facet_grid(.~month) + 
  labs(
    x = "Bike Type",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)"
  )
```

Ride durations are strongly right-skewed across all combinations of month, bike type, and membership status: most rides peak around 5–10 minutes and nearly all are under 50 minutes, but there are outliers that stretch the violins out. Thus, for better visualization, I will do another plot restricted to rides less than 50 minutes of ride duration. 

```{r}
citibike |> 
  filter(year == "2024", duration <=50) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = rideable_type , y = duration, fill = member_casual)) + 
  geom_violin() + 
  facet_grid(.~month) + 
  labs(
    x = "Bike Type",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)"
  )
```

Restricting to rides of 50 minutes or less (which excludes `r scales::comma(nrow(citibike |> filter(year == "2024", duration > 50))/nrow(citibike |> filter(year == "2024"))*100)`% of 2024 rides), ride durations are right-skewed in every group, with most rides lasting under 15 minutes. Membership status shows the clearest difference: members’ rides are concentrated around 4–5 minutes, while casual riders’ rides peak slightly later and are spread more widely across 10–30 minutes. This difference is largest for classic bikes. For members, the distributions look similar for classic and electric bikes, whereas casual riders take somewhat longer rides on classic bikes than on electric bikes. July rides are slightly longer and more spread out than January rides, particularly among casual riders.
